solution:
Let N(d) count triples with a+b+c=60, each divisible by d, and 7 | (a+2b+3c). Such triples exist only for d | 60; writing (a,b,c)=d(x,y,z) gives x+y+z=60/d. If 7 ∤ d, the weighted congruence remains a nontrivial congruence modulo 7. For x+y+z=n, there are (n+1)(n+2)/2 triples, and the value x+2y+3z modulo 7 is uniformly distributed when n=60/d is at least 6: transferring one unit between x and z cycles the weight residues, with boundary-free residue counts equivalently obtained by the roots-of-unity filter. Thus N(d)=(n+1)(n+2)/14. If 7 | d, the congruence is automatic and N(d)=(n+1)(n+2)/2.

Möbius inversion gives the desired count Σ_{d|60} μ(d)N(d). The square-free divisors of 60 are 1,2,3,5,6,10,15,30, with signs +,−,−,−,+,+,+,−. None is divisible by 7, so the count is 1/14 times [61·62 − 31·32 − 21·22 − 13·14 + 11·12 + 7·8 + 5·6 − 3·4] = 138.
insight: Möbius inversion over the common divisor converts the gcd-one condition into an alternating sum over divisors of 60.
insight_justification: For each triple, the sum of μ(d) over its common divisors is 1 when its gcd is 1 and 0 otherwise, so summing these weights enforces the gcd condition exactly.
